name: Bhaktapur
tagline: Khwopa, the city of potters, drums and the five-roofed Nyatapola
meta_description: Bhaktapur (Khwopa) with locals: Nyatapola, Durbar Square, Pottery Square, juju dhau, Bisket Jatra, where to stay and why to spend a night in the old town.
summary: Bhaktapur, Khwopa in Nepal Bhasa, is the best preserved of the valley's three royal cities, 13 km east of Kathmandu. It has three great squares, the five-tiered Nyatapola, open-air potters and a famous sweet curd. Stay at least one night to see it at dawn and after the day visitors leave.
intro: Bhaktapur feels like a working town that happens to be full of temples. Cars are restricted in much of the old core, so the sounds are of hand looms, dhime drums practising for a festival, potters' wheels and grain being threshed on the paving. Farmers still walk out each morning to fields at the town's edge, and many families have lived in the same tole for generations.

The town has three main squares. The Durbar Square holds the 55-Window Palace and the Golden Gate. Taumadhi has Nyatapola, at about 30 m the tallest temple in Nepal, and the Bhairav temple beside it. Tachupal, the oldest quarter, has the Dattatreya temple and the carved Peacock Window. Between them run lanes of brick houses with carved windows, sunken water spouts and small ponds.

Bhaktapur suffered badly in the 2015 earthquake, losing houses and several temples. Much has been rebuilt by local craftsmen, partly paid for by the visitor fee the municipality charges at its gates. The fee is higher than elsewhere in the valley, and it shows: streets are cleaner, restoration more careful and the old town more intact than anywhere else in Nepal.

story.title: The old capital that kept its own ways
paras: Tradition credits King Ananda Deva Malla with founding or expanding Bhaktapur in the 12th century, and for about three centuries it was the capital of the whole valley. After King Yaksha Malla died in 1482, his heirs divided the kingdom and Bhaktapur became one of three rival cities. Its kings were great builders: Bhupatindra Malla raised Nyatapola in 1702 and much of the palace; Jaya Ranjit Malla added the Golden Gate in 1754.

Bhaktapur was the last of the three cities to fall to Prithvi Narayan Shah, in 1769. It then sank into a quiet farming town while Kathmandu grew. That neglect saved it. When the German-funded Bhaktapur Development Project began in 1974, it restored temples and installed drains and paving, but the town's layout and life were largely unchanged. Today Bhaktapur still speaks Nepal Bhasa first.

The 1934 earthquake had already destroyed much of the old palace, and the 2015 quake brought down the Vatsala Durga temple, Fasidega and many houses. Nyatapola, built on a stepped stone base, survived both. Rebuilding has been led by the municipality and local craftsmen, using the visitor fees. Walk the lanes now and you will see brand new carved windows next to old ones, set in walls of salvaged brick.

legend: Local legend says Bhairav, the fierce form of Shiva in his temple at Taumadhi, grew restless and troubled the town. King Bhupatindra Malla was told to build a temple for a goddess stronger than Bhairav, so he raised Nyatapola for Siddhi Lakshmi beside Bhairav's shrine. People say the king carried the first bricks himself, and that the stone guardians on its stairs grow ten times stronger with each step, ending with the goddesses at the top.
people: Bhaktapur is a Newar town, and Nepal Bhasa is its daily language. Jyapu farming families work the fields at the edge of the town, Prajapati families make pots in their courtyards, and woodcarvers, metalworkers and painters keep their trades alive. The town's festival life depends on guthis and on families such as the Banmala, who dance the Navadurga masked dances. Many younger people now work in Kathmandu but return for every jatra.

untold.fact: The stone guardians on Nyatapola's five stair platforms are arranged so each pair is said to be ten times stronger than the pair below: two legendary wrestlers, then elephants, lions, griffins and finally the goddesses Baghini and Singhini.

Bhaktapur was the capital of the whole Kathmandu Valley until the late 15th century. Only after King Yaksha Malla's death in 1482 did the kingdom split into the separate city-states of Bhaktapur, Kathmandu and Patan.

From 1974 to the mid-1980s, the German-funded Bhaktapur Development Project paved streets, built drains and restored temples, one of the first large urban conservation projects in Nepal. Its work is a reason the old town is so intact.

Large two-sided Newar drum played in festival processions
Open public rest house, often run by a guthi

taste.name: Juju dhau
taste.text: The king of curds: buffalo milk boiled down, sweetened and set in unglazed clay bowls, so it turns thick, creamy and slightly caramel. Buy it fresh from small shops round the Durbar Square and Taumadhi, eaten with a spoon from the bowl. Mornings are best, before the day's batch sells out.

facts: Nyatapola, Pottery Square, juju dhau, Bisket Jatra

highlights.title: Taumadhi and Nyatapola
highlights.text: Climb the steep stairs of the five-roofed Nyatapola past its stone guardians, then sit on the steps and watch the square. The Bhairav temple stands beside it. Cafes on the square's upper floors look across both temples.

highlights.title: Durbar Square and the Golden Gate
highlights.text: The 55-Window Palace, the gilded Golden Gate of 1754 leading to the Taleju courtyard, and a row of rebuilt stone and brick temples. Mornings are quietest; school groups arrive by late morning.

highlights.title: Pottery Square
highlights.text: In Talako, potters throw bowls, pots and piggy banks on hand-spun wheels, and set hundreds out to dry in the sun on the paving. Watch, try a wheel, and buy a small pot from the maker.

highlights.title: Tachupal and the Peacock Window
highlights.text: The oldest quarter of town, centred on the Dattatreya temple. In a lane nearby, the Pujari Math has a carved wooden window with a fanned peacock, one of the most famous in Nepal. A woodcarving museum is next door.

highlights.title: Siddha Pokhari at the gate
highlights.text: A large rectangular pond at the western entrance to the old town, from the Malla period, with fish, egrets and elderly men on benches. A good place to start a walk or end the day.

highlights.title: Bisket Jatra in April
highlights.text: Bhaktapur's New Year festival, when the chariots of Bhairav and Bhadrakali are hauled through the streets by competing halves of the town and a tall pole is raised and pulled down. Loud, crowded and exciting.

how_to_reach.text: Bhaktapur is 13 km east of central Kathmandu. A taxi or private car takes 45 minutes to an hour, longer in rush hour, via the Araniko Highway or Kausaltar. Local buses leave from Ratnapark and Bagbazar in Kathmandu for the Bhaktapur bus park near Siddha Pokhari, taking about an hour. The old core is mostly closed to cars.

A popular walk links Changunarayan and Bhaktapur: about 2 hours downhill through fields and villages from the temple to the old town. From Nagarkot, the walk via Telkot and Changunarayan takes most of a day.

where_to_stay: Stay inside the old town if you can. Small guesthouses and boutique hotels in restored Newar houses cluster round Taumadhi, the Durbar Square and Tachupal, and many have rooftop terraces looking over the temples. Rooms are simple to mid-range; book early for Bisket Jatra in April. Larger hotels sit along the main road outside the core. Many travellers combine a Bhaktapur night with Nagarkot, 45 minutes up the hill.
tips: Keep your Bhaktapur ticket; with your passport, it can be extended for longer stays at the ticket office.
Arrive by 7 am or stay overnight to see locals at puja, and the squares before groups arrive.
Buy juju dhau in the morning, when it is fresh and the shops have full stock.
Ask potters before photographing them close up, and buy a small piece if you spend time at a wheel.
Wear shoes with grip; brick paving is slippery after rain and steep on Nyatapola's stairs.

experiences.title: Bhaktapur's three squares with a local guide
experiences.summary: A morning walk linking Bhaktapur's Durbar Square, Taumadhi and Tachupal through the lanes between them. We see the Golden Gate, Nyatapola, the Bhairav temple, Dattatreya and the Peacock Window, with stops at water spouts, rest houses and family courtyards.
body: We start at the Durbar Square, in front of the 55-Window Palace and the Golden Gate of 1754, the gilded doorway to the Taleju courtyard where only Hindus may enter. We explain what fell here in 1934 and 2015, which temples are rebuilt and which are originals, and what the stone pillars and bells were for.

Then we walk down to Taumadhi, where Nyatapola rises on its five-stepped base, its stairs flanked by guardians. Beside it, the broad Bhairav temple is the home of the god pulled through the streets at Bisket Jatra. We stop for juju dhau or tea, and look at the chariot sheds and the small Til Mahadev temple tucked behind.

Finally we follow the old main street east to Tachupal, the oldest part of town. The Dattatreya temple faces a square of monasteries, and in a lane nearby the Pujari Math has its famous carved Peacock Window. On the way we pass dyers, weavers and a water spout where women wash clothes, and step into a courtyard or two.

faqs.q: How much is the Bhaktapur entry fee?
faqs.a: Foreign visitors pay a heritage fee at the gates, which has been about NPR 1,500 to 1,800 in recent years; SAARC and Chinese visitors pay less. The ticket covers the whole old town and can be extended for longer stays with your passport. Fees change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Bhaktapur better than Kathmandu Durbar Square?
faqs.a: For many travellers, yes. Bhaktapur is quieter, cleaner and more complete as a town, with fewer cars and more daily life in its squares. Kathmandu has the Kumari and the big markets. If you only have time for one heritage city, choose Bhaktapur or Patan.

faqs.q: Can I climb Nyatapola temple?
faqs.a: You can climb the stairs of the stepped base to the top platform, past the stone guardians, for views over Taumadhi. The temple interior is closed to visitors and is opened only to priests. The steps are steep and narrow, so take care, especially with children or after rain.

experiences.title: Throw a pot in Bhaktapur's Pottery Square
experiences.summary: Spend a morning with a Prajapati potter in Talako, the pottery quarter just south of Taumadhi. Watch pots thrown on hand-spun wheels and set out to dry, then try the wheel yourself and learn how kilns of straw and ash are fired.
body: Bhaktapur's potters belong mainly to the Prajapati community, and their quarter is a small square south of Taumadhi known as Pottery Square. On dry mornings the paving is covered with rows of drying pots, water jars, piggy banks and oil lamps. Potters spin heavy wheels by pushing them with a stick, then throw the clay while the wheel turns.

We sit with a family potter, who shows how clay from the valley's fields is soaked, trodden and kneaded, and how a pot is thrown, trimmed and stamped. Then you try the wheel. It is harder than it looks, and most first pots collapse, which the potters find very funny. You can keep a piece if it survives.

We also look at how the pots are fired in open kilns of straw and ash, which you may see smoking in a corner of the square, and talk about how the trade is changing with plastic and steel. Buying a small piece directly from the maker is the best way to support the craft.

faqs.q: Can I try pottery in Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: Yes. Several potter families in Pottery Square let visitors try the wheel for a small fee, usually 20 to 45 minutes with help. It is best on dry mornings from October to May. Book through a guide if you want a longer session with a particular family.

faqs.q: Where is Pottery Square in Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: It is in Talako, a few minutes' walk south-west of Taumadhi and the Nyatapola temple, inside the old town. Locals call it the potters' square. Look for rows of drying pots on the ground and smoke from the straw kilns.

faqs.q: Is Pottery Square good for children?
faqs.a: Very. Children love watching the wheels and trying to throw a pot, and the square is car-free. Keep them from stepping on drying pots, which cover much of the ground, and bring wet wipes for clay-covered hands. A small pot or piggy bank makes a good souvenir.

experiences.title: Juju dhau, bara and Khwopa's snack shops
experiences.summary: A late-afternoon food walk through Bhaktapur's squares and lanes: juju dhau from the clay bowl, bara and chatamari off the griddle, chhoyla with beaten rice, and Bhaktapur's own fried sweets. We eat where townspeople eat, and finish as the temples are lit.
body: Bhaktapur is famous across Nepal for juju dhau, the king of curds, and every Kathmandu family that visits takes a bowl home. We start at a small dairy near the Durbar Square, where buffalo milk is boiled and sweetened and set in unglazed clay bowls that draw off moisture. The result is thick enough to hold a spoon upright.

From there we walk to Taumadhi and its lanes for savoury khaja: bara, the black-lentil patty cooked on a flat pan, chatamari, the rice-flour crepe, and chhoyla, spiced grilled buffalo, served with beaten rice and a sharp tomato or potato pickle. We also try local fried snacks and a cup of milk tea.

As the light fades, the shrine lamps start to come on and dhime drummers sometimes practise in the squares. We end on a rooftop above Taumadhi, looking at Nyatapola against the evening sky, with a last bowl of curd or, for those who want it, a glass of aila, the Newar rice spirit.

faqs.q: What is juju dhau?
faqs.a: Juju dhau means king curd in Nepal Bhasa. It is a sweet, thick yoghurt from Bhaktapur, made from boiled, sweetened buffalo milk set in clay bowls, which draw off moisture and give a firm, creamy texture. It is eaten as a dessert or at festivals, and sold in bowls of several sizes.

faqs.q: Where can I buy juju dhau in Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: Small dairy shops around the Durbar Square, Taumadhi and the bus park sell it in clay bowls. Buy it in the morning or early afternoon, when it is freshest. Carry it flat; the clay bowls are fragile. It keeps for about a day without a fridge.

faqs.q: Is Bhaktapur food spicy?
faqs.a: Some of it. Chhoyla, achar and many Newar pickles are spiced with chilli and timur pepper, a numbing Sichuan-style peppercorn. Bara, chatamari, beaten rice and juju dhau are mild. Ask for less chilli (piro kam) and your guide will order to taste.

experiences.title: Dawn in Khwopa's toles and water spouts
experiences.summary: An early walk for those staying overnight: neighbours at morning puja, women at the stone spouts, farmers heading out with hoes, and the squares empty of visitors. Best light for photographs, and the best time to feel how the town really lives.
body: Bhaktapur wakes early. By 6 am in autumn, people are walking to their neighbourhood shrine with small plates of rice, flowers, vermilion and a bell, touching each god on the way. We follow that circuit through the toles round Taumadhi and Tachupal, stopping wherever something is happening.

Water spouts are the centre of morning life. At sunken hitis, carved with makara heads, women fill copper and plastic pots and wash vegetables, and men wash before work. We explain how the spouts were fed by old channels from the hills, and why some have dried up as groundwater has dropped.

As the sun rises, farmers set off with hoes towards the fields east of town, tea shops fill and the first school children appear in uniform. The squares are still almost empty of visitors, and the low light on brick and gilded roofs is at its best. We finish with tea and fried breakfast bread before you head back for breakfast.

faqs.q: Is it worth staying overnight in Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: Yes. Day visitors arrive from about 9 am and leave by late afternoon. If you stay, you see the town at dawn and after dusk, when locals reclaim the squares and the lamps are lit. Guesthouses inside the old town are simple to comfortable and many have rooftop views.

faqs.q: What time does Bhaktapur open?
faqs.a: The old town is a living town and never closes; the ticket booths on the main approach roads operate from early morning to evening. If you stay overnight, your ticket covers your stay. Some museums and palace areas keep shorter hours, roughly 9 am to 4 or 5 pm.

faqs.q: Can I photograph people at puja in Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: Wide shots of a square at dawn are fine. For close portraits, especially of people praying, ask first with a gesture and accept a no. Do not step in front of someone offering at a shrine, do not use flash, and never touch offerings or ritual objects.

faqs.q: How far is Bhaktapur from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: About 13 km east of central Kathmandu. By taxi or private car it takes 45 minutes to an hour, more in rush hour. Local buses from Ratnapark and Bagbazar take about an hour and stop near Siddha Pokhari, at the edge of the old town. It also makes a good stop on the way to Nagarkot.

faqs.q: How much time do I need in Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: Half a day covers the three squares and Pottery Square. A full day lets you eat, wander the lanes and visit the woodcarving museum. We recommend one night, so you see the town at dawn and dusk. Two nights works well with a day trip to Changunarayan or Panauti.

faqs.q: What is Bhaktapur famous for?
faqs.a: Bhaktapur is known for its well-preserved old town, three squares of Malla-era temples, the five-roofed Nyatapola, Pottery Square, the Peacock Window, juju dhau curd, and festivals like Bisket Jatra and Gai Jatra. It is part of the Kathmandu Valley UNESCO World Heritage Site.

faqs.q: Was Bhaktapur damaged in the 2015 earthquake?
faqs.a: Yes. Several temples, including the Vatsala Durga temple in the Durbar Square, and many houses collapsed or were damaged. Nyatapola survived. Most monuments have been rebuilt, partly with entry-fee income, and the town is fully open, though you will see some construction.

faqs.q: Why is the Bhaktapur entry fee higher than other sites?
faqs.a: The Bhaktapur municipality sets its own fee and uses it for heritage conservation, cleaning and services in the old town. The fee covers the whole town for your visit and can be extended for longer stays. Fees change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: When is the best time to visit Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: October and November are clear and pleasant. March and April are warm, and mid-April brings Bisket Jatra, the town's biggest festival. Gai Jatra, in August or September, is longer and more theatrical here than in Kathmandu. Monsoon is wet but the town is quiet.

faqs.q: Is Bhaktapur safe to walk alone?
faqs.a: Yes. The old town is lived in, compact and generally very safe by day and evening. Take normal care with valuables in crowds during festivals. Lanes are poorly lit at night and paving is uneven, so use a phone torch and watch for steps and drains.

faqs.q: Can I combine Bhaktapur and Nagarkot?
faqs.a: Yes, they pair well. Spend a day and night in Bhaktapur, then drive 45 minutes up to Nagarkot for sunset and sunrise. Or walk from Nagarkot down via Telkot and Changunarayan to Bhaktapur in most of a day, an easy descent through villages and forest.

faqs.q: What should I buy in Bhaktapur?
faqs.a: Clay pots and lamps from Pottery Square, woodcarvings and miniature windows from the workshops round Tachupal, handmade paper, and Bhaktapur-woven cloth. Juju dhau is the edible souvenir. Buy from makers where you can, and ask for a receipt for larger pieces.
